questions.question_text: Which of the following brain regions is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery?
questions.explanation: ACA supplies the medial surfaces of the frontal lobes, including the genu and body of the corpus callosum. PCA supplies cuneus, inferior temporal and lingual gyri. MCA supplies planum temporale.

questions.question_text: Which region of cerebral blood flow correlates with hallucinations and delusions?
questions.explanation: Auditory hallucinations and delusions in schizophrenia correlate with reduced grey matter density and activation in the left medial temporal cortex (superior temporal gyrus).

questions.question_text: The role of ependymal cells is:

options.text: Lining the walls of the ventricular systems

correct_answer.text: Lining the walls of the ventricular systems

correct_answers.text: Lining the walls of the ventricular systems

questions.explanation: Ependymal cells line the ventricles of the brain and contribute to cerebrospinal fluid circulation via their cilia. Specialized ependymal cells form the choroid plexus.

questions.question_text: The disengagement of attention is mediated by:
questions.explanation: The parietal lobe, particularly the medial parietal cortex, is involved in shifting attention (disengagement). Early Alzheimer’s disease affects this region and causes attentional deficits.

questions.question_text: Which neuroglial cells act as scavenger cells at the sites of CNS injury?
questions.explanation: Microglia are CNS macrophages derived from blood monocytes and act as scavenger cells, removing debris after neuronal injury.

questions.question_text: Which of the following enzymes is seen only in the neuron and not in glial cells?
questions.explanation: Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) is neuron-specific and used as a marker for GABAergic neurons. Glutamine synthase is found in glia.

questions.question_text: MAO-A is available primarily in which of the following body tissues?
questions.explanation: MAO-A is predominantly expressed in the gastrointestinal tract and heart. MAO-B is more abundant in the brain.

questions.question_text: The most common side effect when using sildenafil is
questions.explanation: Viagra is an indirect vasodilator, resulting in headaches. Common side effects of phosphodiesterase inhibitors (such as sildenafil and tadalafil) are mild headaches, dizziness, and nasal congestion.

questions.question_text: Low CSF concentration of 5-Hydroxy Indole Acetic Acid is associated with which of the following
questions.explanation: Animal and human research suggests that the central serotonin system is involved in the inhibition of impulsive behaviour A low CSF 5-HIAA concentration was primarily associated with impulsivity. Much of the clinical data relating 5-HT and impulsivity have been provided by investigations of suicide. Early studies reported lower CSF and plasma 5-HIAA levels as well as blunted prolactin response to fenfluramine in both suicide attempters and completers, as well as lower brain 5-HT, 5-HT transporter, and abnormal 5-HT receptor binding at post-mortem in suicide completers.

questions.question_text: Nitric oxide is synthesized from which of the following
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine when stimulated by nitric oxide synthase. L-arginine is the substrate for nitric oxide synthases, which then produces nitric oxide and L-citrulline.

questions.question_text: Which of the following human spongiform encephalopathy has the slowest course
questions.explanation: Kuru is a type of prion disease which has the slowest course. The incubation period was prolonged—up to 40 years before disease onset, which was then rapid and fatal.

questions.question_text: Mr. X is a 73-year-old gentleman with 5-year history of Parkinson's disease, cognitive decline and visual hallucinations. Post mortem evidence suggests alpha-synuclein deposits and cytoplasmic inclusions. The common microscopic finding expected in this case would be
questions.explanation: The clinical features are suggestive of Parkinson’s disease dementia. The Lewy body is a weak eosinophilic, spherical, cytoplasmic inclusion consisting primarily of alpha-synuclein.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neuroimaging finding is most suggestive of Alzheimer's disease

options.text: Activation of primary auditory cortex on functional MRI
Increased signal in the Pulvinar nucleus of thalamus bilaterally
Medial temporal atrophy on structural MRI scan

correct_answer.text: Medial temporal atrophy on structural MRI scan

correct_answers.text: Medial temporal atrophy on structural MRI scan

questions.explanation: MRI in Alzheimer's disease often shows atrophy of grey matter involving the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex and amygdala in the medial temporal lobe.

questions.question_text: Which neural structure is strongly implicated in the regulation of P50 suppression, a proposed endophenotype in schizophrenia
questions.explanation: P50 suppression is regulated by wide-ranging neural circuitry, prominently involving hippocampal structures. Patients with schizophrenia show deficits in sensory gating measured by P50 suppression.

questions.question_text: A 56-year-old lady with depression, somatic pain symptoms and constipation for weeks, and serum calcium 15.8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism often presents with hypercalcemia, somatic symptoms (constipation, pain), and neuropsychiatric features such as depression and cognitive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements with regard to alpha waves in the EEG is correct

options.text: It is maximal over occipital region
Excess of alpha rhythm is seen in Huntington's disease
It is a higher frequency band than beta waves

correct_answer.text: It is maximal over occipital region

correct_answers.text: It is maximal over occipital region

questions.explanation: The alpha brain waves oscillate at 8–13 Hz, are maximal over the occipital regions, and are reduced by eye opening.

questions.question_text: With respect to depression seen in patients with schizophrenia, which of the following is correct

options.text: It is seen only in post-psychotic period
It is not an outcome indicator
It often coexists with negative symptoms
It is often a side effect of antipsychotic use
It does not respond to antidepressants

correct_answer.text: It often coexists with negative symptoms

correct_answers.text: It often coexists with negative symptoms

questions.explanation: Affective symptoms occur commonly in non-affective psychosis, and up to half of individuals with post-psychotic depression also meet criteria for negative symptoms, indicating overlap.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to posttraumatic stress disorder? (according to ICD-10 criteria)

options.text: Onset is within 6 months of trauma
Trauma must be near fatal in nature

correct_answer.text: Onset is within 6 months of trauma

correct_answers.text: Onset is within 6 months of trauma

questions.explanation: The onset of PTSD is generally within six months of the trauma. Retrospective reports of war veterans reveal that delayed-onset PTSD is extremely rare one year post-trauma, and there was no evidence of PTSD symptom onset six or more years after trauma exposure.

questions.question_text: Select one typical feature of hypomania
questions.explanation: As defined in ICD-11, a hypomanic episode is a persistent mood state lasting at least several days characterised by mild elevation of mood or increased irritability and increased activity or subjective experience of increased energy, accompanied by other characteristic symptoms such as rapid speech, rapid or racing thoughts, increased self-esteem, an increase in sexual drive or sociability, decreased need for sleep, distractibility, or impulsive or reckless behaviour. The symptoms are not severe enough to cause marked impairment in occupational functioning or in usual activities or relationships with others, do not necessitate hospitalisation, and there are no accompanying delusions or hallucinations.

questions.question_text: What is the most common psychiatric disorder in children with mild intellectual disability?
questions.explanation: Disruptive and conduct-disorder behaviours occurred more commonly in the mildly disabled group, which represents approximately 85 percent of persons with intellectual disability. ADHD is often a prominent feature in children with ID. Those with severe mental retardation have a particularly high rate of autistic disorder and pervasive developmental disorders.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman believes that her neighbours are plotting to kill her for the last 6 months. There is no hallucination. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Delusional disorder is an illness characterized by the presence of nonbizarre delusions in the absence of other mood or psychotic symptoms. Delusional disorder is characterised by the development of a delusion or set of related delusions, typically persisting for at least 3 months and often much longer, in the absence of a depressive, manic, or mixed mood episode. The delusions are variable in content across individuals, but typically stable within individuals, although they may evolve over time. Other characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia (i.e. clear and persistent hallucinations, negative symptoms, disorganised thinking, or experiences of influence, passivity, or control) are not present, although various forms of perceptual disturbances (e.g. hallucinations, illusions, misidentification of persons) thematically related to the delusion are still consistent with the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Chomes has recently lost her husband after his protracted fight with stomach cancer. Which of the following is indicative of a pathological grief disorder?

options.text: Persistence of grief response for more than 12 months after his death
Joining a charity for fighting prostate cancer
Clearing his room of his belongings

correct_answer.text: Persistence of grief response for more than 12 months after his death

correct_answers.text: Persistence of grief response for more than 12 months after his death

questions.explanation: Prolonged grief disorder is a disturbance in which, following the death of a partner, parent, child, or other person close to the bereaved, there is a persistent and pervasive grief response characterised by longing for the deceased or persistent preoccupation with the deceased accompanied by intense emotional pain (e.g. sadness, guilt, anger, denial, blame, difficulty accepting the death, feeling one has lost a part of one’s self, an inability to experience positive mood, emotional numbness, difficulty in engaging with social or other activities). The grief response has persisted for an atypically long period of time following the loss (more than 6 months at a minimum) and clearly exceeds expected social, cultural, or religious norms for the individual’s culture and context. The disturbance causes significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Some degree of mummification (preserving the belongings of the deceased as they were before death), visual hallucinations of the deceased ('sighting the dead'), altruistic charity and seeking help through counseling are normal reactions.

questions.question_text: In ICD-10 astasia-abasia is described under:
questions.explanation: In ICD-10 dissociative (conversion) disorders are classified into dissociative amnesia, dissociative fugue, trance/possession, disorders of movement (includes motor disorders), dissociative stupor, dissociative convulsions (pseudoseizures) and dissociative sensory loss/anaesthesia. Astasia-abasia is discussed under dissociative motor disorders.

questions.question_text: A university student has been diagnosed with Kleine Levin syndrome after presenting with recurring periods of excessive drowsiness and sleep. Which of the following feature is NOT a part of this diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Drop attacks are not a part of Kleine Levin syndrome. Kleine-Levin syndrome (KLS) is a rare disorder characterised by periodic episodes of hypersomnolence and hyperphagia. Other behavioural symptoms may occur, including sexual disinhibition, confusion, irritability, restlessness, euphoria, hallucinations, delusions, and schizophreniform states.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is included in the new diagnostic grouping of disorders of bodily distress and bodily experience in ICD-11?
questions.explanation: The diagnostic grouping of disorders of bodily distress and bodily experience includes bodily distress disorder, which broadly replaces somatoform disorders and neurasthenia, and body integrity dysphoria, which is characterised by the desire to have a certain disability. The other diagnoses lie within the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders.

questions.question_text: Mr Richmond obtains gratification by rubbing against women travelling on the crowded Dockland Railways. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: Frotteuristic disorder is characterised by a sustained, focused, and intense pattern of sexual arousal—as manifested by persistent sexual thoughts, fantasies, urges, or behaviours—that involves touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person in crowded public places. The individual must act on these thoughts or be distressed by them. It excludes consensual touching or rubbing.

questions.question_text: When asked how many legs a cat has, a 42-year-old male prisoner answers 'five legs'. Which of the following conditions is likely?
questions.explanation: Vorbeireden (also known as 'talking past the point') is seen in Ganser syndrome. It refers to the production of 'approximate answers' in which the content of the patient's replies shows understanding of the question but answers with unrelated or incorrect information. Ganser syndrome includes approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations or pseudohallucinations, motor disturbances, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness.

questions.question_text: A middle aged man presents with 2 year history of having abnormal limb movements and memory problems. He has no past history of psychiatric problems and physical investigations are unremarkable. His father died at the age of 50 and he had similar 'limb shakes'. The likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease onset is defined by the beginning of motor symptoms, often chorea or choreoathetosis (irregular writhing and jerking movements). It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern due to CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene; alleles with 40 or more repeats are fully penetrant.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of schizoid personality disorder?

options.text: Highly sensitive and intolerability to setbacks

questions.explanation: Clinical features of schizoid personality disorder include a preference for solitude, indifference to social norms and conventions, lack of desire for close relationships, restricted range of emotional expression, and indifference to praise or criticism from others.

questions.question_text: According to DSM-5 criteria, which of the following is not included in the diagnostic criteria for a manic episode?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 criteria for a manic episode require a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and persistently increased activity or energy, plus three (or more) of: inflated self-esteem or grandiosity; decreased need for sleep; more talkative than usual; flight of ideas; distractibility; increased goal-directed activity; excessive involvement in activities with high potential for painful consequences. 'Increased need for sleep' is NOT a criterion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following diagnostic groupings includes selective mutism in ICD-11?
questions.explanation: In ICD-11, Anxiety and fear-related disorders include selective mutism and separation anxiety disorder.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old man presents to the memory clinic with a MMSE score of 23/30. What will you do in terms of management?

options.text: Repeat memory test in 3 months time
Arrange for dementia screen work up

correct_answer.text: Arrange for dementia screen work up

correct_answers.text: Arrange for dementia screen work up

questions.explanation: An MMSE score of 23/30 suggests possible cognitive impairment. Arrange a dementia work-up including blood tests, urine analysis, ECG, and brain imaging (CT or MRI).

questions.question_text: Physical findings that point to a metabolic cause of mental status change include
questions.explanation: Asterixis (flapping tremor) is a sign of metabolic encephalopathy. It is elicited by having the patient extend both arms with wrists dorsiflexed; brief jerky downward movements of the wrists indicate a positive sign.

questions.question_text: On examination, there is a repeated fluctuant movement of agonist and antagonist muscles when the patient tries to reach something. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: This describes an intention tremor, which is characteristic of cerebellar lesions. The tremor worsens as the patient approaches the target due to impaired coordination.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following eye signs is pathognomonic of multiple sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is highly suggestive of MS in young patients. INO results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, causing impaired adduction and abducting nystagmus.

questions.question_text: A 64 year old lady has a history suggestive of frontal lobe dementia. Which of the following bedside cognitive tests is appropriate to assess frontal lobe function?
questions.explanation: The category fluency test (e.g., naming as many animals as possible in one minute) is a quick bedside test of executive/frontal lobe function. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Test is a detailed neuropsychological assessment.

questions.question_text: Intention tremor is characteristically seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: An intention tremor is a kinetic tremor that worsens as the patient approaches a visual target, due to cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the single most useful tool for diagnosing dementia?

options.text: Clinical interview of patient and carer

correct_answer.text: Clinical interview of patient and carer

correct_answers.text: Clinical interview of patient and carer

questions.explanation: A thorough clinical interview of the patient and carer remains the cornerstone of dementia diagnosis; no test can replace clinical assessment.

questions.question_text: Read the strip of ECG shown below and identify the relevant abnormality. P waves are marked in the figure.

options.text: Type I second degree heart block

questions.explanation: In complete heart block (third-degree AV block), there is complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity. P waves and QRS complexes bear no relationship, and a ventricular escape rhythm is present.

questions.question_text: Amnesia refers to marked impairment in
questions.explanation: Amnesia refers to a marked impairment in episodic memory (memory of events), with relative preservation of procedural, semantic, and working memory.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old girl loved to help her mother in kitchen. She was scared of going near the cooker after she burnt her hand. This is explained by
questions.explanation: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when the conditioned stimulus no longer produces the conditioned response. Here, the kitchen/cooker no longer elicits approach behaviour after it was paired with a painful burn.

questions.question_text: Which type of reinforcement is the least resistant to extinction?
questions.explanation: Continuous reinforcement (reward after every response) is most easily extinguished once the reward is removed. Intermittent schedules, especially variable ratio, are more resistant.

questions.question_text: A psychologist takes a 31 year old patient with significant fear of heights to the top of a 21 storey-building. Which of the following behavioural technique is he employing?
questions.explanation: Flooding involves immediate and prolonged exposure to the feared stimulus in vivo (actual situation) until the anxiety subsides, leading to extinction of the fear response.

questions.question_text: In patients with moderate head injury, post traumatic amnesia is usually expected to last
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) duration of 1 to 24 hours indicates moderate head injury. PTA less than 1 hour is mild, and more than 24 hours is severe.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding operant conditioning is correct?

options.text: It cannot be used in patients with learning disability as the concept of reward is non-existent in most patients
Punishment is the most effective form of operant learning
It is a form of associative learning
It was first described by Albert Bandura
Negative reinforcement refers to introducing an aversive stimulus to reduce the frequency of a behaviour

correct_answer.text: It is a form of associative learning

correct_answers.text: It is a form of associative learning

questions.explanation: Operant conditioning (like classical conditioning) is a form of associative learning. Habituation and sensitisation are non-associative. Punishment only suppresses responses; negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour. Albert Bandura described social learning theory, not operant conditioning.

questions.question_text: Which statement among the following about short-term memory is false?

options.text: The retrieval process in short term memory is error free.
Information is held in the STM for 15 to 30 seconds.
It can be extended by rehearsal
Chunking of material can effectively increase the capacity of short term memory
It is mainly stored in the visual modality

correct_answer.text: It is mainly stored in the visual modality

correct_answers.text: It is mainly stored in the visual modality

questions.explanation: Short-term memory encoding is primarily acoustic (auditory), not visual. Information is held for 15–30 seconds, can be extended by rehearsal, chunking increases capacity, and retrieval is relatively error free.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a behavioural component of Allport's concept of prejudice?
questions.explanation: Allport described prejudice as having cognitive (stereotype), affective (hostility), and behavioural components. Discrimination (actions against a group) is the behavioural component.

questions.question_text: A police officer arrives at a place to investigate a reported crime. He notices a suspicious looking man who looks at the officer and runs away without talking to the officer. The police team arrests him out of suspicion and is not ready to listen to any of his explanations. But he turns out to be not guilty as the investigation proceeds. Which of the following is a likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Halo effect is the tendency to perceive other persons as wholly good or bad based on few observed traits. Investigators may wrongly associate suspects with attributes seen in other criminals, causing guilt by association.

questions.question_text: Which of the following instruments could be used to measure the discriminant attitudes and level of stigma in a community?

options.text: Community attitudes to mental illness scale

correct_answer.text: Community attitudes to mental illness scale

correct_answers.text: Community attitudes to mental illness scale

questions.explanation: The Community Attitudes to Mental Illness (CAMI) scale measures attitudes across authoritarianism, benevolence, social restrictiveness and community mental health ideology.

questions.question_text: According to Holmes and Rahe's social readjustment rating scale (SRRS) which one was rated as the most serious life event?
questions.explanation: Holmes and Rahe rated 'Death of a spouse' as the most serious life event in their list of 43 events, with minor law violations rated as least serious.

questions.question_text: Koro can be classified as a/an:
questions.explanation: Koro’s fear of genital shrinkage is phenomenologically a desomatisation phenomenon (false change in body part size or shape).

questions.question_text: A Sri Lankan man presents with depression and fatigue, and attributes it to excessive masturbation and losing semen in urine. What is the name of his condition?
questions.explanation: Dhat syndrome is characterised by anxiety and hypochondriacal concerns associated with semen loss, leading to weakness, fatigue and guilt.

questions.question_text: At what age can a child build a tower of 6 cubes?
questions.explanation: By age 2, a child can run and build a tower of six cubes. By age 3, they can typically build a tower of nine to ten cubes.

questions.question_text: Mastering intimate relationships despite the demands of work is a successful developmental task for ages between
questions.explanation: Erikson’s stage of Intimacy vs. Isolation occurs between ages 20 and 40, focusing on forming lasting intimate relationships.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to day-care for children?

options.text: 4 months day care before age 1 for more than 20 hours/week may be detrimental
Regular day care affects cognitive development

correct_answer.text: 4 months day care before age 1 for more than 20 hours/week may be detrimental

correct_answers.text: 4 months day care before age 1 for more than 20 hours/week may be detrimental

questions.explanation: Belsky and Rovine (1988) found insecure attachments were more likely if a child received more than 20 hours/week of day care for at least four months before age one.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants is associated with a significant risk of agranulocytosis compared to the others listed?
questions.explanation: Drugs ending in ‑zapine (e.g., mirtazapine, olanzapine, clozapine) and the tetracyclic mianserin are known for risk of agranulocytosis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants has a recognized side effect of elevated cholesterol?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine has been associated with hyperlipidaemia, similar to olanzapine.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a dystonia?
questions.explanation: Tics are not classified as dystonia. Dystonias involve sustained or repetitive muscle contractions, unlike the brief, sudden movements of tics.

questions.question_text: Veronica has been going through a period of change and is feeling stressed. She finds it especially difficult to get to sleep after drinking three cups of coffee before bed. Which is the main neuro-receptor implicated in her struggle to get to sleep after caffeine?
questions.explanation: Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist. Adenosine binding normally promotes sleepiness; blocking it increases alertness.

questions.question_text: Shaun is an 11-year-old child diagnosed with epilepsy. His parents report angry outbursts and destructive behaviour. Which antiepileptic is most likely associated with behavioural disturbances?
questions.explanation: Vigabatrin has been linked to behavioural disturbances in children, with studies reporting rates as high as 26%.

questions.question_text: Carol stops paroxetine abruptly and experiences tiredness, muscle aches, headaches and nausea for about a week. What is a proposed mechanism for SSRI discontinuation syndrome?

options.text: Temporary deficiency in the brain of one or more essential neurotransmitters associated with mood
Temporary excess in the brain of one or more essential neurotransmitters associated with mood
Long-standing changes to brain structure which reduce capacity to produce these neurotransmitters
Release of inflammatory proteins producing flu-like symptoms

correct_answer.text: Temporary deficiency in the brain of one or more essential neurotransmitters associated with mood

correct_answers.text: Temporary deficiency in the brain of one or more essential neurotransmitters associated with mood

questions.explanation: The syndrome is thought to result from a sudden drop in serotonin (and possibly other neurotransmitters) leading to withdrawal symptoms.

questions.question_text: Paul on risperidone has galactorrhea and prolactin 960 MIU/L. Which dopamine receptor is most implicated in raised prolactin?
questions.explanation: Antipsychotic blockade of D₂ receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway disinhibits prolactin release, causing hyperprolactinemia.

questions.question_text: Antonio has poorly controlled diabetes and takes captopril for hypertension. He is now manic and needs a mood stabiliser. Which should be avoided considering his renal issues and ACE inhibitor use?
questions.explanation: Lithium is renally excreted and interacts with ACE inhibitors, risking reduced clearance and toxicity.

questions.question_text: Mrs Myrtle on depot antipsychotic sometimes kicks her husband in bed and can’t sit still in a chair. What is the best fitting description?
questions.explanation: Akathisia is a movement disorder from antipsychotics characterised by inner restlessness, pacing, and inability to sit still.

questions.question_text: Mr Farah was psychotic, restrained and given an antipsychotic injection. Two hours later he is pyrexic, hypertensive, confused, with muscle rigidity. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome is a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics with rigidity, fever, autonomic instability, and altered mental state.

questions.question_text: Mr Hicks on clozapine presents with fever and chest pain. What ECG changes would you see in clozapine-induced myocarditis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine-induced myocarditis shows diffuse ST-segment elevation (saddling), T-wave inversion and other non-specific changes.

questions.question_text: Sally, with Huntington’s disease, has worsening chorea. Which medication is most likely to be prescribed for her movement disorder?
questions.explanation: Tetrabenazine depletes monoamines and is approved for chorea in Huntington’s disease and other hyperkinetic disorders.

questions.question_text: Mr Brown, an alcoholic, received 10 mg diazepam from his daughter before presentation. Which is true regarding diazepam’s pharmacokinetics?

options.text: Protein binding 98% with main active metabolite desmethyldiazepam
Protein binding 98% with temazepam as the main active metabolite
Protein binding 98% with no active metabolites
Protein binding 65% with main active metabolite desmethyldiazepam
Protein binding 65% with no active metabolites

correct_answer.text: Protein binding 98% with main active metabolite desmethyldiazepam

correct_answers.text: Protein binding 98% with main active metabolite desmethyldiazepam

questions.explanation: Diazepam is ~98% protein bound. Its principal active metabolite is desmethyldiazepam; minor metabolites include oxazepam and temazepam.

questions.question_text: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency is associated with increased sensitivity to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Donepezil should be avoided in pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Succinycholine and mivacurium (muscle relaxants) also cause prolonged paralysis.

questions.question_text: Caffeine is a commonly used psychoactive substance. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding caffeine?

options.text: Saliva concentration is half of plasma level
It is more damaging to fetus in rapid metabolisers than slow
It is metabolised similarly in all ethnic groups

correct_answer.text: Saliva concentration is half of plasma level

correct_answers.text: Saliva concentration is half of plasma level

questions.explanation: Caffeine concentrations in saliva and plasma are similar. It is primarily metabolised by CYP1A2 (with minor contributions from other P450s). Clearance varies by ethnicity and fetuses are more affected in rapid metabolisers.

questions.question_text: The blood–brain barrier permits selected molecules through. Which of the following does it allow through?
questions.explanation: L-DOPA crosses via the L-type amino acid transporter. Generally small, lipophilic, gas molecules or those with specific transporters cross the barrier.

questions.question_text: Serotonin metabolism involves several enzymes. Which of the following is NOT involved in serotonin metabolism?
questions.explanation: COMT degrades catecholamines (dopamine, noradrenaline) but not serotonin, which is degraded by MAO and aldehyde dehydrogenase after deamination.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is acceptable to take along with MAO inhibitors?
questions.explanation: Foods like cheese, broad beans, red wine and pickled herring contain tyramine and risk hypertensive 'cheese reaction'. Grapefruit juice does not.

questions.question_text: Which route of administration leads to nicotine reaching the brain fastest?
questions.explanation: Inhalational delivery (smoking) reaches the brain faster than sublingual, intravenous, cutaneous or oral routes.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about reboxetine is correct?

options.text: Reboxetine is a hepatic enzyme inhibitor
Reboxetine is a hepatic enzyme inducer
It does not affect hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
It is completely excreted via kidneys

correct_answer.text: It does not affect hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes

correct_answers.text: It does not affect hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes

questions.explanation: Reboxetine is metabolised in the liver but does not inhibit or induce cytochrome P450 enzymes.

questions.question_text: An orally administered medication requires five half-life periods to reach steady state concentration. Which of the following is most likely correct about this drug?

options.text: Doses up to five times the normal are non-toxic
A loading dose must be provided for adequate therapeutic activity
Its rate of metabolism is independent of its concentration
This medication must be administered only once a day

questions.explanation: Under first-order kinetics, at least 5 half-lives are required to reach steady state. Zero-order kinetics elimination is concentration-independent.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to sodium valproate?

options.text: Intravenous preparation is available for acute mania
It is excreted unchanged via kidney
It has no significant interactions with other mood stabilisers
Should not be combined with antidepressants

questions.explanation: Valproate inhibits glucuronidation of carbamazepine, raising its peak levels and risk of dose-related side effects. It also interacts with lamotrigine and chlorpromazine.

questions.question_text: Regarding pharmacokinetics and properties of flumazenil, which of the following is true?

options.text: It is an inverse agonist at GABA receptor
It has an elimination half-life of 4 hours
It is a partial agonist at GABA receptor

questions.explanation: Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist of benzodiazepines at benzodiazepine sites of GABA-A receptors. By blocking GABA-A neurotransmission, it can precipitate seizures, making it an epileptogenic drug. It has no agonist activity in humans and a short elimination half-life (~40–80 minutes), requiring infusion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is hydroxylated as one of the steps in dopamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Dopamine synthesis begins with hydroxylation of L-tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase, producing L-DOPA, which is then decarboxylated to dopamine.

questions.question_text: A 63-year-old man with mood disorder is on ramipril for hypertension. Which of the following drugs is most likely to interact?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors like ramipril reduce renal excretion of lithium, increasing lithium levels and risk of toxicity. Co-prescription requires close monitoring.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to pharmacology of lithium?

options.text: Lithium is unsafe in the elderly
Lithium is contraindicated in patients with sick sinus syndrome
Obesity is associated with lower rates of lithium clearance
It is not excreted in breast milk
Lithium cardiotoxicity is more prevalent in people on a high-salt diet

correct_answer.text: Lithium is contraindicated in patients with sick sinus syndrome

correct_answers.text: Lithium is contraindicated in patients with sick sinus syndrome

questions.explanation: Lithium is contraindicated in patients with sick sinus syndrome due to risk of conduction disturbances. It is safe in the elderly with monitoring, excreted into breast milk, clearance is renal and not affected by BMI, and toxicity is more likely with low salt intake.

questions.question_text: What WAIS subtest is most resistant to brain damage?
questions.explanation: ‘Hold’ subtests (e.g. Vocabulary, Information, Picture Completion, Object Assembly) tap crystallised knowledge and resist brain injury. ‘No-hold’ subtests (Digit Symbol, Digit Span) decline earlier.

questions.question_text: A 43-year-old man with pure word deafness is likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Meaning of words is intact when asked

questions.explanation: Pure word deafness (auditory verbal agnosia) features impaired comprehension of spoken words with preserved reading, writing and nonverbal auditory processing.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following tests is not correctly linked with the main function tested?

options.text: Benton Visual Retention Test – Visual memory
Rey-Osterrieth Figure – To detect prefrontal lobe pathology

correct_answer.text: Rey-Osterrieth Figure – To detect prefrontal lobe pathology

correct_answers.text: Rey-Osterrieth Figure – To detect prefrontal lobe pathology

questions.explanation: The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test assesses visuospatial constructional ability and visual memory, not specifically prefrontal pathology.

questions.question_text: There is a time gradient in retrograde amnesia where recent memories are lost more than remote memories. This is called:
questions.explanation: Ribot's Law (1881) describes temporally graded retrograde amnesia in which newer memories are more vulnerable than older ones.

questions.question_text: The most obviously affected neuropsychological measure in post-concussion syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Processing speed deficits are the most prominent and consistent finding in individuals with post-concussion syndrome.

questions.question_text: A patient with an UMN lesion of cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII would most likely have:
questions.explanation: UMN lesions of glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves cause spastic dysphagia (swallowing difficulty); chewing (V) and facial sensation (V) are spared; fasciculations indicate LMN.

questions.question_text: To measure impairment of everyday memory functioning for rehabilitation, the most suitable test is:
questions.explanation: The Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test uses everyday memory tasks to detect and monitor functional memory problems.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with alcohol dependence is disorganized but has no memory or neurological signs. He would likely show impairment on:
questions.explanation: Alcohol-related executive dysfunction is reflected in impaired performance on Trail Making Tests, which assess set-shifting and cognitive flexibility.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old man has a 10-hour episode of complete anterograde/retrograde amnesia, appears bewildered, then returns to normal. Diagnosis:
questions.explanation: Transient global amnesia is an abrupt, reversible episode of profound, isolated anterograde amnesia (and variable retrograde amnesia) lasting up to 24 hours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cannot be termed a reliable endophenotype for schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Endophenotypes must be heritable, state-independent markers that co-segregate with illness; clinical symptom clusters (e.g. negative symptoms) do not meet these criteria.

questions.question_text: Which statement is least likely about Huntington's disease?

options.text: Huntingtin gene codes for huntingtin protein
CAG repeat size and age at onset are inversely correlated
Late-onset HD is usually inherited from mother
Paternally derived gene may be more unstable than maternally derived gene
Normal huntingtin gene has 35–45 CAG repeats

correct_answer.text: Normal huntingtin gene has 35–45 CAG repeats

correct_answers.text: Normal huntingtin gene has 35–45 CAG repeats

questions.explanation: Normal alleles have 7–28 CAG repeats. Individuals with 29–35 are intermediate; ≥40 are fully penetrant.

questions.question_text: Where does transcription take place in human cells?
questions.explanation: Transcription of DNA into RNA occurs in the nucleus, in discrete ‘transcription factory’ sites.

questions.question_text: Probandwise concordance rate is calculated as:

options.text: Number of total pairs divided by the affected population
Number of twin pairs divided by total sib pairs
Number of affected twins divided by total number of co-twins
Number of twin pairs divided by total relatives
Number of twin pairs divided by total population

correct_answer.text: Number of affected twins divided by total number of co-twins

correct_answers.text: Number of affected twins divided by total number of co-twins

questions.explanation: Probandwise concordance = (number of affected co-twins) / (total number of co-twins), used in systematically ascertained twin studies.

questions.question_text: Which gene knockout produces mice with a narcolepsy phenotype?
questions.explanation: Knockout of hypocretin/orexin genes in mice produces narcolepsy-like symptoms including cataplexy and fragmented sleep.

questions.question_text: The technique used to assemble correct DNA fragments from a gene library into a continuous overlapping stretch is:
questions.explanation: Physical mapping uses overlapping DNA fragment sequences to order and assemble large genomic regions.

questions.question_text: What is the best test for diagnosing Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: PCR is used to determine CAG repeat length in the HTT gene, confirming a diagnosis of Huntington's disease.

questions.question_text: Polyploidy refers to which phenomenon?

options.text: Presence of one or more extra sets of chromosomes
Reduplication of nuclear material before cell division

correct_answer.text: Presence of one or more extra sets of chromosomes

correct_answers.text: Presence of one or more extra sets of chromosomes

questions.explanation: Polyploidy denotes cells or organisms with more than two homologous sets of chromosomes (e.g., triploid 3n, tetraploid 4n).

questions.question_text: Recombination occurs during which phase of meiosis?
questions.explanation: Crossing-over (genetic recombination) occurs in prophase I of meiosis during synapsis of homologous chromosomes.

questions.question_text: Ribosome is the site of:
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are the cellular machinery for translating mRNA into polypeptides (protein synthesis).

questions.question_text: A 53-year-old gentleman with progressive short-term memory loss, gradual onset, MMSE 17/30. The gene most likely involved is:
questions.explanation: Early-onset familial Alzheimer’s disease is often caused by mutations in presenilin-1 (PSEN-1). ApoE4 is a risk allele for late-onset AD.
